turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Afternoon. You've been kept waiting, I know, we're all over the place today. Is this the repeat prescription review?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, and not before time. My knee is murdering me and those tablets aren't touching it. I want something stronger.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been on about it all week. I'm June, I live in and do the caring.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks, June. So it's the knee, and you want the pain relief looked at. Which knee?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): The right. Always the right one. About six years, since I packed the job in. Worse on the stairs, and when it's cold and damp.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee, about six years, worse on stairs and in the cold. Is the pain there all the time?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): All the time. And it wakes me in the night. I'm worn out with it, if I'm honest.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She was up pacing at about three. I made tea and she still couldn't settle.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain all the time, waking you, and you're tired with it. Any stiffness in the mornings?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Stiff as a board. Twenty minutes or so, then it eases if I walk about the kitchen. Um, after that it's just the ache.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can you talk me through the tablets you're actually taking?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, two of the five-hundreds, four times a day. Naproxen five hundred, morning and night. The stomach one, omeprazole, twenty, well, actually I nearly said ten then, no, it's twenty, with breakfast. And amlodipine five milligrams for the blood pressure.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The lunchtime paracetamol often doesn't happen. If she's napping, or we're out, that one gets missed. I do the morning and evening pots.

[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the midday paracetamol is hit and miss. I've got the list the pharmacy technician left on the desk. It says naproxen two hundred and fifty milligrams twice a day, not five hundred. The rest matches: paracetamol one gram four times a day, omeprazole twenty milligrams once a day, amlodipine five milligrams once a day.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): That list is wrong. I've been on the five hundred naproxen for ages. Don't tell me it's two fifty.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I don't handle that box, she does, so I can't say which is printed on it.

[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to guess between two hundred and fifty and five hundred. I won't put a naproxen dose on anything until the pharmacy confirms it. Please don't take any extra while we sort it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I still want something that works. Codeine. Or tramadol, like my neighbour takes. Paracetamol's useless.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): I hear that. Before we talk about stronger tablets, any dizziness, or any falls?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The stairs are the real problem. Coming down is agony, I have to do them one at a time.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): The stairs, yes. I'm asking about dizziness and falls though. Have you had any?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No dizziness, no falls. Head's clear.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No falls that I've seen. She uses the rail.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your stomach, on the naproxen, any burning, or black stools?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Did I mention the damp? It sets the knee off something rotten. Worse than the stairs some days.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll note the damp. Burning in the stomach, or black stools, yes or no?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No burning. And the stools are normal, brown, thank you.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or anything else?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Nothing I've ever been told. No allergies.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Apart from the osteoarthritis and the blood pressure, any other problems, any operations?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations. Just the arthritis in that knee and the blood pressure. My mother had terrible knees, ended up stuck in a chair.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mother with severe knee trouble. Do you smoke, or drink?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Gave the fags up when I retired, that's ten years. One whisky on a Sunday, if there's any in.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): One measure, I pour it. And I'm there at night, she's not on her own.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me look at the knee. Can you get onto the couch?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): If I must. Watch the right one, it doesn't like being shoved.

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee, no swelling I can see. Tender along the inside joint line, and it creaks when I bend it. Left knee is quiet, nothing like that. Pulse is seventy-eight, blood pressure one hundred and thirty-six over eighty-four.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): There. Not in my head, is it.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nobody said it was. This fits the osteoarthritis we already know about, flaring a bit, not a new problem in the joint. I am not adding codeine or tramadol. They make people drowsy and constipated and more likely to fall, and they won't mend the knee.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): So I just put up with it.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. Keep the paracetamol regular, including that midday dose. Don't put the naproxen up, and don't add ibuprofen from the chemist on top of it. Omeprazole stays at twenty milligrams every morning, amlodipine at five every morning. I'll reauthorise those three as they are. Naproxen stays on hold.
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can put an alarm on for the lunchtime paracetamol.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): If you must. I'm sick of alarms.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): While I get these typed, that telly in the waiting room was on the cricket. Did you see any of it?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Waste of an afternoon. England were all over the shop. Bloke at slip put down two catches in one over, I nearly turned it off.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She did have a go at the remote. The receptionist gave us a look.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): And don't get me started on getting here. Roadworks on the ring road, sat behind a cement mixer for twenty minutes, then your car park was full and we went round twice.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): The ring road's been a mess for a fortnight. I came the back way, past the allotments.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Allotments. Next door's growing marrows the size of rugby balls and handing them over whether you want them or not. Soup three days running.
[SEG0053] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The soup was all right, to be fair to him.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): You can have the next one, then. I'm done with marrow.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, back to this before we lose it. Paracetamol one gram four times a day, try not to skip lunchtime. Omeprazole twenty milligrams each morning. Amlodipine five milligrams each morning. No change to the naproxen and no extras until we know if it's two hundred and fifty or five hundred. No codeine, no tramadol. A bit of gentle walking, and that moving about in the morning already helps the stiffness, so keep that up.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I still think you're being tight with the strong ones.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): I know you do. I'm not prescribing them today. If the pain suddenly gets much worse, or you get black stools or stomach pain, come back sooner, don't wait. Otherwise I'll see you in three months for the next repeat review.
[SEG0058] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll ask at the desk about the three months, and I'll ring the chemist about the naproxen box.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Three months. Wonderful. Can we go? I'm tired and my knee's had enough of that couch.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, off you go. June, if the chemist comes back with a figure that isn't two fifty or five hundred, ring us before she changes what she takes.
